newsitem.title: UK: Scotland's E coli outbreak claims 20th victim.
newsitem.headline: Scotland's E coli outbreak claims 20th victim.

text.p: An elderly woman became the 20th victim of Scotland's outbreak of food poisoning on Sunday, making it the worst ever caused by the virulent modern strain of the E coli bacteria.

She was one of hundreds of people who caught the bacteria in central Scotland last November and December. "She was an elderly lady who didn't fully recover," said a spokeswoman for the Forth Valley Health Authority.

"All the deaths are from the same outbreak. I understand that she is the 20th victim and that it is the worst outbreak in the world so far," the spokeswoman said. She did not name the victim, who died in a nursing home in Banknock, north of Edinburgh.

E coli was a normally harmless digestive bacteria until it developed a virulent form identified 15 years ago. It gets into food via improper slaughtering and hygiene techniques or when manure is used as fertiliser.
Most of the Scottish cases have been traced to a shop owned by a local butcher who has been accused of reckless conduct in connection with a supply of contaminated meat.
E coli can make a healthy adult ill but small children and the elderly can succumb to kidney failure and brain damage.
There have been hundreds of cases of E coli infection in the United States and Canada which were linked to apple juice. The deadliest outbreak was in Canada in 1985 when 19 elderly people died.
Earlier this year Britain's former Conservative government denied that it had suppressed a report on unhealthy conditions in the country's abattoirs which could have contributed to food poisoning.

The report prepared by hygiene service officer Robert Swann in 1995 on the conditions in slaughterhouses found that animal faeces were finding their way onto carcasses being prepared for human consumption. The faeces can harbour the E coli bacteria.

Former agriculture minister Douglas Hogg, who was highly criticised for his handling of the mad cow crisis, told parliament in March that the document had been redrafted, but had been made available to meat industry officials.

Swann told the Financial Times newspaper, which leaked the report, that if his recommendations were carried out uniformly in Britain's 600 slaughterhouses "the risk from E coli...would be considerably diminished."
